Additionally, she was advised to avoid vigorous physical activity for 4 weeks.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 8-year-old girl sustained blunt chest trauma from a scooter handlebar strike to the chest wall while riding in her front yard. She initially experienced only mild localized chest wall pain and continued playing. Approximately 24 hours post-injury, she developed lightheadedness and two presyncopal episodes while standing in the classroom. EMS found an intermittent faint and rapid pulse with a wide rapid rhythm consistent with ventricular tachycardia on the rhythm strip. On ED presentation, she was hemodynamically stable, denied chest pain/shortness of breath/palpitations, and was found to have multiple runs of stable non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (longest ~10 seconds) with monomorphic accelerated ventricular rhythm of LBBB morphology on ECG. Troponin I and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable. Cardiac MRI on hospital day 2 confirmed the diagnosis, revealing right ventricular myocardial contusion with focal areas of delayed enhancement, oedema, significant regional wall motion abnormalities involving the right ventricular outflow tract and free wall (RVEF 41%), a subacute precordial haematoma, and a small pericardial effusion with possible pericardial haematoma. The left ventricle was normal with LVEF 69%. She was started on verapamil 40 mg every 8 hours on arrival; the dose was increased to 60 mg every 8 hours on hospital day 3 due to sustained frequent ectopic beats. By hospital day 4, PVCs had decreased in frequency, and she was cleared for discharge by the pediatric cardiology electrophysiologist. She was discharged on verapamil with instructions to follow up with pediatric cardiology in 2 weeks, a Holter monitor was ordered, and she was advised to avoid vigorous physical activity for 4 weeks.
